Chapter 29. February: The Tuner and the Hand.

spans.text: The Olympic Air from Athens to Kos was the fifty-five-minute morning route, the kind of hop that left before the city had quite warmed.

Phaedon Trakas had been on Olympic since seven on the seventeenth of August 2026. His grandmother had taken him to the airport at five-thirty. She had not stayed. He did not yet know that the pencil under the bench at Cleopatra Street would be at his hand by the seventy-year mark; he was eighteen and at the curb at half past five.
She had said at the curb of the departures terminal: Phaedon mou.
He had said: Yiayia.
She had said: the wood-and-mother-of-pearl box.
He had said: I have it.
She had said: Alexandria carried it out in 1962.
He had said: I know, Yiayia.
She had said: Pothia will take it for four years.
He had said: I know.
She had said: Carrier Press told me at the program-interview feedback letter in March that there is a piano at the Drosos dorm under a tarp.
He had said: I had not been told.
She had said: the piano has been at the Drosos front room since the 1953 delivery from the Alexandria piano-builder's Pothia cooperative.
He had said: yes.
She had said: the Alexandria piano-builder was Loukas Trakas.
He had said: Yiayia.
She had said: Loukas Trakas was my great-grandfather. Your great-great-grandfather.
He had said: I had not been told.

She had said: I had not told. The piano at the Drosos front room is the first of the twelve he built for the cooperative from 1948 to 1956. I am telling you at five thirty-five in the morning on the seventeenth of August 2026 because the four years at Pothia and Alexandria will be at the piano.
He had said: yes, Yiayia.

She had said: the Trakas name has been at the piano-bench storage in the 1948 letter since the 1953 delivery. Yiayia Marigoula will show you the letter when the house decides you are at the bench-storage week.
He had said: yes.
She had said: go.
He had walked into the departures terminal. He had not looked back. She had not waved.

The departures hall at five forty-three on Tuesday morning held the kind of Athens-pre-dawn light a glass-roofed atrium kept before the airport had quite filled: a fluorescent grey-and-white at the boarding screens, the smell of fresh bread from the upper-level kiosk three minutes after the bakery opened, the early-summer warmth already at the windows facing the runway. He counted the people at the Olympic counter line and rounded to eight. He counted the bars he would have at the piano in the first hour at Pothia, three movements of a Bach two-part invention, and rounded to forty. The numbers sat in his head at the kind of weight a Tuesday-pre-dawn airport could hold without effort.

He checked one suitcase. He kept the smaller suitcase with the box. He walked to gate fourteen at six. He sat at the row of plastic chairs against the south wall. He read four pages of L'Étranger in the French. He stopped at the page where Meursault, asked about the funeral, answered in the way he answered. He marked the margin in pencil at the second line of the answer and closed the book.
The Olympic from Athens to Kos was half empty at the Tuesday-morning hop.

He boarded at six twenty and took 14F at the window. He had read L'Étranger in the French. He had read it fourteen times since his thirteen-year-old acquisition; the French was his second tongue from his mother's Italian-school years in Athens between 1968 and 1980. He stopped at page forty-seven at the Meursault-mother-funeral-walk passage, marked the margin in pencil, closed the book, drank an orange juice. He counted fifteen passengers. The engines under the cabin sat somewhere around an A-flat, ground-bass, ritardando whenever the pilot eased the throttle.

He kept the A-flat at the back of his head for the duration. He let the cabin announcements sit a half-step above it (a B-flat, the safety-recording voice carried the kind of practised flatness Greek airline-women had been carrying since his mother had first taken him on Olympic at four), and the rustle of the man across the aisle at the in-flight Kathimerini sat a fifth below the engine-ground (an E-flat, slightly under, ragged at the page-turn). The three pitches gave him a chord he did not need to resolve, and the chord ran for the duration of the climb.
He landed at Kos at eight forty.

The shuttle bus from the airport ran on platform two at nine fifteen. The wait at the platform was the kind of Kos-airport wait the August Aegean heat made into a full hour: he sat at the bench under the eucalyptus tree at the platform's south end, drank the half-bottle of water from his carry-bag, watched the two German couples ahead in the queue manage a stroller. He was at the Mastichari ferry dock at nine forty. He bought the hydrofoil ticket at the kiosk and boarded at ten fifteen. He counted twenty-three passengers. He read four more pages of L'Étranger. The ferry pulled into Pothia harbor at five past eleven.

The Pothia harbor at five past eleven on Tuesday the seventeenth of August 2026 held the late-summer Aegean dry warmth at the dock, the brine-and-bougainvillea air the Mediterranean kept for arrivals.

He walked off the ferry with his two suitcases. The dock at the north side held nine sponge boats, three kafenia, six dock-workers. The kafenia owners had set the morning chairs at the long shaded plank under the awning of the middle kafenia, To Limanaki, and four old men sat at the chairs with backgammon-boards open and Greek-coffee cups at the table-edge; one of them looked up at the ferry and looked back at his board without changing the rhythm of his hand. The dock-greeter at the east end was a short young man in a clean white shirt with a placard:
PHAEDON TRAKAS Year 1, Cohort B, Drosos house, Vouvalis Street
Phaedon walked to him.
He said in Greek: Phaedon Trakas.
The young man said: Stelios Vouvalis.
Phaedon said: Stelios.
Stelios said: welcome to Pothia.
Phaedon said: thank you.
Stelios said: the Drosos house at Vouvalis Street, four minutes' walk.
Phaedon said: all right.

Stelios took the larger of the two suitcases. Phaedon kept the smaller, which held the wood-and-mother-of-pearl box. They walked from the dock to the house. The walk took four minutes. Stelios said three things in the four minutes, in the kind of Pothia-island Greek a twenty-three-year-old bakery-son spoke. He said the white house at the third turning was the Pappadakis family. He said the harbor was at its August quiet and the September would bring the sponge boats back from the Sfax-and-Libyan beds. He said the Drosos house was at the seventy-third year of Yiayia Marigoula's tenure. Phaedon said yes at each of the three. The fourth turning brought them to Vouvalis Street, and the painted-blue door of the Drosos house was at the third building on the right.

The Drosos house had a painted-blue door, a front courtyard, an old olive tree, bougainvillea on the south wall. Stelios knocked at the painted-blue door. Yiayia Marigoula, eighty-two, opened it at the first knock.
She said: Phaedon Trakas.
He said: Yiayia Marigoula.
She said: welcome to Pothia.
He said: thank you, Yiayia.
She said: come in.

He came in. The front hall held three objects at the walls: a 1947-parish-festival photograph at the east wall (forty-three figures around the parish priest, two of them Marigoula at three and Marigoula's mother Marioula at thirty-three, the priest a Kalymnos-Pothia parish-elder Phaedon's grandmother had named at the Nea-Smyrni kitchen when he was nine), a Theotokos icon at the south wall (the gilt at the halo had a Pothia-island patina the Athens-icon-painters did not produce), a wooden hat-rack at the north wall (six pegs, three coats at three pegs, an umbrella at one peg, the other two pegs empty). Yiayia Marigoula walked him to the dining room at the back. A wooden table at the centre, six chairs at the sides. He was the first of the five to arrive.
She said: the first arrival.
He said: yes.
She said: Niko Lekkas the twentieth from Darwin. Lina Belhadj-Kosma the twenty-second from Sfax. Tia Theodorakis the twenty-fourth from Broome. Athena Markou the twenty-seventh from Tarpon Springs.
He said: yes.
She said: ten days at the Drosos house with the Yiayia and Stelios and no other cohort.
He said: ten days.

She said: the first-arriving cohort-mate has been at the front-room piano in the first week, every cohort since 2008. The piano sits at the north corner under the dust-cover. It was at the Drosos house since the 1953 delivery. The program-application letter named the piano.
He said: yes, Yiayia.
She said: Stelios will show you to the east-side second-floor bedroom.
He said: yes.

She said: the Sponge Industry Museum at Sofia Kassotis at the second of September, ten days after the cohort gathers. The cohort orientation at the kitchen at four on the twenty-eighth. The kitchen rules at the kitchen.
He said: yes, Yiayia.
She said: the kitchen rules at the kitchen. Stelios.
Stelios said: Yiayia.
She said: the bedroom.
Stelios said: yes, Yiayia.

The bedroom on the east side of the second floor was a square room with a bed at one wall, a wooden desk at the east-facing window, a wardrobe. The wardrobe held a new linen-and-cotton sheet set Yiayia Marigoula had laid in on the Monday afternoon. Stelios set the larger suitcase on the floor at the foot of the bed.
Stelios said: the bedroom.
Phaedon said: thank you, Stelios.

Stelios said: the front-room piano sits at the north corner of the ground-floor front room. Yiayia Marigoula has said it is yours to find in the first week. Dinner in the kitchen at seven. Yiayia Marigoula and me.
Phaedon said: yes.

Stelios said: the bakery at four in the morning. Konstantinos Vouvalis at the kitchen and the oven; me at the second oven and the delivery round at six. The bakery closes at one. I am at the Drosos house at two. The Yiayia is at the back-flat kitchen at most afternoons, and at the front kitchen at four and onward.
Phaedon said: yes.
Stelios said: the four years at Pothia. The Drosos house has had this rhythm since 2008. You will find it.
Phaedon said: I will find it.
Stelios said: all right.
Stelios walked out. The door closed at twelve fifteen.

Phaedon unpacked the larger suitcase. He put clothes in the wardrobe. He set five books on the shelf above the wooden desk: L'Étranger, Cavafy's Poems in bilingual Greek-French, La Recherche volume one in French, Le Comte de Monte-Cristo in French, Carlo Levi's Cristo si è fermato a Eboli in Italian. He set a framed photograph of Yiayia Areti at thirty-six at the Nea-Smyrni piano in 1986 on the bedside table. He set a second framed photograph (his mother Aurelia at twenty-four in Trieste at the Carafà-family piano in 1980, three months before her Athens-conservatory move and her Trieste-Carafà-final-summer) on the south side of the wooden desk.

He took the wood-and-mother-of-pearl box from the smaller suitcase. He set it at the corner of the wooden desk. The box was ten inches by six, the lid inlaid with mother-of-pearl. It was Yiayia Areti's great-grandmother's box, carried out of Alexandria in 1962 at the twelve-year-old Areti's emigration. It held four items: two photographs (the Trakas family at the 1933 Alexandria Cleopatra-Street balcony, and Areti at twelve at her 1962 Athens arrival), a folded two-page piano arrangement of the Alexandrian song in Loukas Trakas's 1933 handwriting, and an empty perfume bottle his mother's mother had bought in Alexandria in 1955.

Phaedon stood at the corner of the desk. He placed his two hands at the box. He let them sit at the lid. He took them off after a minute. He did not open the box. The box had been at the Nea-Smyrni kitchen for sixty-four years, and the lid had been opened at four occasions Yiayia Areti had named to him in the long telling of the box across his childhood years: at her thirteenth birthday in 1963, at her own grandmother Areti-the-elder's passing in 1971, at his mother Aurelia's wedding to his father Manolis in 1986, and at his own seventh birthday in 2013 when the folded sheet music had come out for the first reading. The fifth would be at his hand, in his time. He did not yet know when.

He walked down at twelve forty. He walked from the front hall to the front room on the east side of the ground floor. The front room held a couch at the north wall, the piano under its dust-cover at the north corner, two armchairs at the east-facing window. A wall-screen had been set on the south wall above the bookcase; the bookcase held two shelves of Greek-island parish histories and one shelf of Pothia-cohort program records since 2008.

The tarp was a cotton sheet Yiayia Marigoula had put over the piano in 2010 when the cohort program moved the front-room screen for the Zoom calls. The piano had been at the Drosos house since the 1953 delivery from the Trakas Alexandria piano-shop. It was the first of the twelve in the Loukas-Trakas Pothia cooperative arrangement. It was his great-great-grandfather's piano.
He pulled the cover at the back. It came away slowly. He folded it on the floor beside the piano.
The piano was a Bechstein-style baby-grand of Loukas Trakas's 1953 build, with a brass plaque on the soundboard side:
Trakas Piano. Alexandria. 1953.

He set his two hands on the key-cover and lifted. The keys were original ivory and ebony, clean (Yiayia Marigoula had wiped them at the first Saturday of August in the annual ritual). He sat at the bench.
He placed his hands at the keyboard and played a slow C-major scale.

The piano had been at the Pothia-Drosos front room for seventy-three years in the Mediterranean-island climate, with the annual cleaning but no tuning since the cohort program had paused in 2010. The middle C ran flat by about eleven cents; the G above middle C ran flat by about seventeen. The instrument was off by fifteen or twenty cents overall.
The piano needed tuning. He could hear the need.
He played a C-major chord. Detuned. He played G-major. Detuned. He played F-major. Detuned.

He set his hands at his lap. He sat at the bench for a minute. The front room at twelve fifty-five held the late-summer Pothia warmth at the open east-facing window and the smell of bougainvillea from the south wall of the courtyard. A donkey passed on Vouvalis Street outside, two doors west, and the sound of the hoof at the cobble carried into the room at the kind of pitch a Pothia-summer afternoon gave the visiting ear, somewhere around a G-natural slightly above middle C. He held the G-natural a beat. The donkey passed.
He said in Greek: the piano.
The front room did not respond. He laughed three-quarters of a second late. The joke had nobody to share it with. He laughed once more for the nobody.

He played a single bar of the Alexandrian song from the folded sheet music upstairs and from memory of Yiayia Areti at her Nea-Smyrni kitchen piano, where she had played for him between his sixth and seventeenth years. The song was a slow-melodic Aegean-Greek-Alexandrian Trakas family song, kept since his great-grandmother's Alexandria childhood in 1937 and into Areti's 1962 Athens arrival. He played the first eight bars slowly.
The piano was flat. The song was still the song.
He stopped at the end of the eighth bar. He set his hands at his lap. He sat at the bench at five past one on the afternoon of Tuesday the seventeenth of August 2026.

He sat at the bench for ten minutes. He did not play. He looked at the brass plaque on the soundboard side. He looked at the way the wood of the case caught the late-summer light at the east-facing window: the rosewood at the lid had taken on a Pothia-island patina across seventy-three years that the Alexandria-rosewood had not held in his grandmother's Nea-Smyrni-kitchen piano. The piano had been in two cities; it had stayed in one for seventy-three years; it had become a Pothia object without ceasing to be an Alexandria object. He held the doubled-belonging a beat, in the way he held chords without resolving them.
He stood at quarter past one.
He walked back to the dining room at seven minutes past one. Yiayia Marigoula was at the kitchen with a briki.
She said: Phaedon.
He said: Yiayia.
She said: the piano.
He said: the piano.
She said: the first eight bars.
He said: yes.
She said: it needs tuning.
He said: it needs tuning.
She said: the tuner is at the Athens conservatory. The post-summer Athens visit. I will arrange the first of September.
He said: yes, Yiayia.
She said: all right.

She poured him a Greek coffee. He drank. She drank. The kitchen at quarter past one held the late-summer warmth at the back-porch door and the smell of the olive tree at the front courtyard. The briki sat at the back ring of the gas hob at a low blue flame; she would pour a second briki at the half-past mark, in the way she had been pouring two briki at the early-afternoon kitchen since 1973 when she had taken over from her mother Marioula.
She said at twenty past one: Phaedon.
He said: Yiayia.
She said: Yiayia Areti and I have been at twice-a-year letter-correspondence since 2000.
He said: I had not been told.
She said: I had not told. Twenty-six years. Areti wrote to me on the fourteenth of August. She said you would be at the piano in the first week.
He said: yes.
She said: the letter is at the back-flat kitchen. I will show it to you at the orientation on the twenty-eighth. The twenty-six years of letters are at the back-flat kitchen drawer.
He said: yes, Yiayia.
She said: all right.

She stood at twenty-five past one and walked to the back porch. She brought in two lemons from the lemon tree at the back garden, set them on the counter, sliced one. The juice ran clear. She poured a glass of water for him and squeezed half the lemon into it. She set it at the table. He drank.

She said at half past one: the Sponge Industry Museum. Sofia Kassotis at the third-floor west room. The cataloguing internship at the new-acquisitions period 2024 to 2026. You at the Tuesday-and-Thursday-and-Friday morning rotation at nine to one starting the eighth of September. Sofia will introduce you on the second.
He said: yes.

She said: Sofia Kassotis is forty-two. She is the museum cataloguer since 2014. Her grandfather worked at the Drosos cooperative storage room in the 1957 to 1962 period. He died in 1995. Her grandmother is at the Pothia upper village. Sofia knew Yiayia Areti's mother Maria-Trakas through a cousin in 1960.
He said: I had not been told.

She said: I had not told. Sofia knows the Trakas-Alexandria piano-shop history through the cousin and the grandfather. Sofia will show you the Drosos-Alexandria correspondence boxes at the storage room in mid-November.
He said: mid-November.

She said: mid-November. The first two Trakas-name letters of the 1957-to-1962 Drosos-Alexandria correspondence are at the new-acquisitions catalogue. You will translate them as the first cataloguing assignment.
He said: yes, Yiayia.
She said: all right.

Dinner in the Drosos kitchen at seven that evening held Yiayia Marigoula at the head, Stelios at the foot, Phaedon on the east side. The three at the kitchen. Yiayia Marigoula cooked yiouvarlakia. They drank water. They ate. Dinner ran from seven to half past eight.

Stelios told Phaedon about the harbor, the bakery on Kalymniou Street, the parish feast at Vathy on the eighteenth of October. He told him about the Pothia upper village and the lower harbor and the way the sponge-boat captains read the August Sfax-and-Libyan weather off the way the cumulus banked at the south-east horizon at four in the afternoon. He told him about the Saturday-evening sponge-museum reception every fourth Saturday, which the cohort sometimes attended. Yiayia Marigoula told him about the Trakas archive at the Year-1 second-internship rotation that his first internship at the Sponge Industry Museum, cataloguing under Sofia Kassotis, would lead into. She told him about the Year-2 municipal-archive internship under Petros Vouvalis (the Pothia-municipal-clerk, Konstantinos Vouvalis's older cousin, fifty-eight). She told him about the cohort-program twenty-six-day post-graduation period the Drosos house had kept since the program's 2008 founding.

Phaedon told them about his grandmother's Nea-Smyrni kitchen, the Alexandrian song, the Trakas Alexandria piano-shop, the 1962 emigration carrying. He told them about his mother Aurelia and her Italian-school years and her conservatory-piano teaching at the Athens conservatory, and about his father Manolis at the Athens-architecture practice on Patriarchou Ioakeim Street, and about his older sister Eirene at Paris with her partner. He did not tell them about the box at the corner of the wooden desk. The box had not yet earned an introduction.
The three finished at half past eight.

Stelios walked to the Vouvalis bakery on Kalymniou Street at nine for the evening shift. (Konstantinos and Stelios kept a four-hour evening shift on Tuesdays and Thursdays at the bakery for the next-morning dough, and Stelios would not be back at the Drosos house until midnight.) Yiayia Marigoula went to the flat at the back at quarter past nine. Phaedon sat on the front-room couch at twenty past nine with a cup of Greek coffee.
The front room held the late-summer warmth at the open east-facing window, the bougainvillea, the piano at the north corner.

He sat for half an hour. He did not play. The keyboard ran in his head at A-equal-440 instead of the fifteen-flat the room had given him; it was easier to hold the corrected version than the real one. Under that ran Loukas at the 1953 Alexandria bench at fifty-three, then Yiayia Areti at twelve at her 1962 Athens arrival with the box at her lap, then the folded sheet music two floors up. He let his mother Aurelia, his father Manolis, his older sister Eirene in Paris and Yiayia Areti's sister Eleni in Paris also stand at the edge of the room without naming them. He let his grandmother's brother Yiannis Trakas (1941-1962, Alexandrian-conservatory classical-guitar, died at twenty-one of Suez-Crisis-related respiratory illness in March 1962) also stand at the edge. The edge held five and his grandmother and Loukas's daughter Maria-Trakas; the edge held seven. He counted them. He let the count rest.
He stood at nine fifty. He walked to the piano. He set his hands at the keyboard. He played the Alexandrian song slowly. The song ran five minutes. The piano was detuned. The song was still the song.
He stopped at five past ten. He sat at the bench a minute. He stood at seven past ten.

He walked up to the east-side second-floor bedroom. He sat at the wooden desk at ten past ten. He took a Moleskine from the front pocket of his backpack and ruled the first page in two columns in pencil. Column one: Greek. Column two: French. He would add a third column for Italian when his mother's tongue was relevant; he would not pre-rule it. He wrote a single line at the head of the first page: ftáno / j'arrive. He closed the Moleskine and set it on the bedside table.

He lay on the bed at half past ten. He looked at the box at the corner of the wooden desk. The four objects in it had a weight he had not measured before, the kind of weight that did not announce itself but stayed. He held the four pictures at the back of his head as a single shape.
The shape was Tuesday the seventeenth of August 2026.
He turned off the lamp at twenty to eleven. He slept seven hours and forty minutes. He woke at twenty past six on Wednesday the eighteenth of August 2026.

The Pothia morning at twenty past six held the late-summer Aegean cool at the east-facing window. The Drosos house was at Phaedon-alone-with-the-Yiayia-and-the-Stelios at the first day of the ten days before the others arrived.
The piano was at the north corner of the front room.
The piano needed tuning.
The tuner from Athens was at the post-summer arrangement.
The carrying.
